blocks.text: 10.2.5 Building the Deterministic Run Harness

Section 10's milestone for GridCap is a promise the planning team can make to its regulator: the same snapshot, solved by the same software with the same settings, gives a byte-identical run manifest, ten times out of ten. Before a plan reaches Budget Lock (lesson 7.1.3), and on every change to the model code, a **run harness** checks that promise and fails loudly when it breaks, saying which field changed so the cause can be found.

The parts are built: fresh processes per run (`repeat.py`, lesson 10.2.1), settings that make each solver repeat (10.2.2), a model whose answer does not depend on luck (10.2.3), and a canonical manifest (10.2.4). This lesson puts them together, runs the harness on HiGHS and CP-SAT, and shows what its failures look like. The model is lesson 10.2.1's, unchanged. GridCap is a fictional utility's portfolio.
The Harness Reruns One Snapshot in Fresh Processes
The harness solves one config several times, and each run is a separate Python process started by `repeat.py`. Lesson 10.2.1 gave the first two reasons; the full list is:

items: **The hash salt.** Each child gets its own `PYTHONHASHSEED` (1, 2, 3, ...), on purpose: a model built from a set's order then gets a different order in each run, and the harness sees the bug instead of hiding it.
**Thread settings that stick to a process.** HiGHS fixes its thread count at the first solve of a process (lesson 4.2.4); runs in one process would all share it.

**Libraries that affect each other.** In this course's runner, importing PuLP in a process makes a later MathOpt HiGHS MIP solve in that same process crash (lesson 5.2.1 shows it). A run in its own process starts with only the imports it needs.
**The real thing.** A nightly job, a service worker, a rerun two years later: each is a new process. A harness that runs the same way tests what will actually happen.

It Compares Whole Manifests, Byte for Byte, and Names What Changed

`check` runs a config `runs` times and compares every manifest with the first, as canonical bytes (lesson 10.2.4). Comparing the whole manifest, not the objective, matters: a tie returns the same objective with another plan (10.2.3), and a clock-limited run can return the same plan after different work (10.2.1). Both are differences a regulator would ask about. Wall time is not in the manifest (lesson 10.2.4 keeps `wall_seconds` apart), so the clock never enters the comparison. When the bytes differ, `diff` walks the two manifests and lists every path where they disagree:

`NotDeterministic` is a subclass of `AssertionError`, so a test that calls `check` fails like any other failed assertion, with the message as its reason. A key that only one manifest has is a difference too: a solver that suddenly reports a new field has changed. `check` stops at the first run that differs from run 1, so it counts nothing: a config passes or it fails.
<!-- practice 1 -->
It Fails Loudly, and the Failure Points at the Cause
`harness.py` runs three configs that should repeat, ten runs each, and then two that should not:

for label, config in good:
        manifest, digest = check(config, runs=10)
        result = manifest["result"]
        print(f"PASS {label}: 10 identical manifests, sha256 {digest[:16]}, "
              f"{result['status']} {result['objective']:,.0f}")

PASS HiGHS, highest NPV, GridCap small: 10 identical manifests, sha256 4fbb9df414248815, OPTIMAL 24,260
PASS CP-SAT, 1 worker, seed 7, GridCap small: 10 identical manifests, sha256 b4da9d6e5c3b3d01, OPTIMAL 24,260
PASS CP-SAT, 4 workers interleaved, seed 7, deterministic limit 2, GridCap medium: 10 identical manifests, sha256 a324a47f0ed56cc3, FEASIBLE 226,469
FAIL HiGHS, most projects, projects in set order, GridCap small:
     run 2 of 5 differs from run 1 at: result.plan, result.plan_digest, result.stats.simplex_iterations

That is the milestone: on HiGHS and on CP-SAT, ten processes with ten different hash seeds wrote byte-identical manifests, including CP-SAT with four interleaved workers stopped by a work limit on GridCap medium. The HiGHS manifest's digest, `4fbb9df414248815`, is the one lesson 10.2.4 printed for the same config: a manifest written in another program, at another time, matched to the byte.

The first failure is lesson 10.2.1's bug, the count question built from a set's order. Read the message as a diagnosis. The status and objective are not in the list, so every run proved the same value; only the plan and the work differ. Same value, different plan: a **tie** picked differently, here by the build order. The fix is in lessons 10.2.1 (build from a sorted order) and 10.2.3 (a tie-break).
The second failure is four CP-SAT workers without interleaving:
FAIL CP-SAT, 4 workers, seed 7, deterministic limit 2, GridCap medium:

The block above ends at the FAIL line on purpose. The program printed a second, indented line with the message, as it did for the first failure, but that line changes each time the harness runs, so the page leaves it out rather than show a line your own run will not reproduce. The message lists the objective, the bound and the plan: the runs did not even agree on how good a plan they found. Under a work limit that points to **threads** racing (lesson 10.2.2's fix: interleave, or one worker).

blocks.text: A Determinism Test Belongs in the Test Suite

A harness that someone has to remember to run will not be run. Put it in the test suite, so that every change to the model code runs it. This module's own tests do that: one test calls `check` on the HiGHS config and the one-worker CP-SAT config of `harness.py` with three runs each and asserts that it returns a manifest; another asserts that the set-order config raises `NotDeterministic`, so the test suite also proves the harness can fail. Three runs on GridCap small take seconds; the ten-run check on the plan of record runs before Budget Lock. Lesson 12.3.4 adds determinism tests of this kind to a full test suite, beside back-tests against past plans.

What the harness proves has limits, and its report should say them. Ten identical manifests show that this config repeats on this software and this machine. They do not show that another machine gives the same plan: a machine with more cores changes Gurobi's default thread count (10.2.2), and Gurobi's determinism article promises the same result only on the same computer, which is why the manifest records `versions.platform`. Run the harness on the image that runs production, and treat a version upgrade as a change that needs a new plan of record, run through the harness again.
<!-- practice 2 -->
Summary

items: **The harness reruns one snapshot in fresh processes,** each with its own hash seed, so set-order bugs, per-process thread settings and library interference show up instead of hiding.
**It compares whole manifests, byte for byte, and names what changed.** The objective alone would miss ties and clock-limited work.
**It fails loudly, and the failure points at the cause.** Same value with another plan means a tie; another value under a work limit means threads; inputs or versions mean a different run.
**A determinism test belongs in the test suite,** with a test that the harness fails on a known bug. Its pass holds for one machine and one version; record both.

Challenges

items: Add a config with a 3-second HiGHS time limit on GridCap medium to the failing list. Predict which fields its message names.
Change `diff` so that it reports which projects were added and dropped when `result.plan` differs. What would the set-order failure then say?
The harness passes on a developer's laptop and fails in CI with only `versions.python` in the message. What happened, and is the plan wrong?

blocks.text: Design Note: A Harness Must Be Able to Fail

A determinism test that has never failed proves nothing about its own strength: it might compare the wrong field, or run everything in one process. That is why `harness.py` and the module's tests include configs that are known not to repeat, and assert that they fail. Keep at least one such known-bad config next to every determinism check you write, and check that it still fails after every change to the harness.

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change.
